C4: The rider's profile (746 days, rating 4.8, zero disputes or upheld flags in 90 days) is clean and supports no penalty against her, while the driver carries 2 upheld disputes in 90 days. [F14 F15] [TH-3]

claims.assertion: The upfront quote was $21.67 at surge 1× (surgeable subtotal $20.20) and the rider was charged $27.82 at a 1.4× multiplier, so the fare is $6.15 above the quote and the whole $6.15 difference arises from the surge multiplier change (the metered distance, 8.6 km, did not exceed the 8.7 km optimal route).

The surge notice at 12:01:40 states only the multiplier and that the rider may cancel for free — it offers a new estimate of $29.75 but no other free-cancellation entitlement is missing; the notice did precede trip start at 12:02:00, so the timing requirement and the three SURGE-1 items (new multiplier 1.4×, revised estimated fare $29.75, free cancellation) appear to be stated.

Even at its highest the refundable surge element is the whole $6.15 the fare exceeds the quote, computed as the excess over the quote capped at the surge-only overcharge; if the court reads the notice as not stating all three items, SURGE-3's differential (or the (1.4 − 1) × $18.82 = $7.53 cap) supports refunding that $6.15 difference, not more.
The rider's profile (746 days, rating 4.8, zero disputes or upheld flags in 90 days) is clean and supports no penalty against her, while the driver carries 2 upheld disputes in 90 days.
The chat record contains two timestamped messages, both about pickup logistics and neither touching the fare or a reroute, so nothing in the exchange shows the rider agreed to pay a surged fare.

The $6.15 claim is under $10, within the system's final jurisdiction for fare disputes, and the only records that could alter the reading — the notice text and the surge log — are present and timestamped, so no missing record need block a ruling.

weaknesses: The surge log F9 records the in-app notice at 12:01:40, before the 12:02:00 trip start, and its text names the new 1.4× multiplier, a revised estimated fare of $29.75 and free cancellation — my own reading of the words is that all three SURGE-1 items are stated, which favours the driver/operator and points to no_action; I do not argue around this record, I read it honestly.

F9 shows the estimate in the notice ($29.75) is higher than the fare finally charged ($27.82) — the notice price was not the price charged, which the other side will say is harmless because SURGE-1 asks only for a stated estimate and the rider was told she could cancel free.

My client's account of the notice arriving 'as I was getting into the car' (the complaint) is a statement contradicted by the platform log F9, and under the conflict rule the system record wins; I cannot build a claim on it.

points.response: Conceded: F1 and F3 show the billed distance of 8.6 km was 0.1 km shorter than the 8.7 km optimal route, so there is no excess-distance deviation and no RD-1/RD-2 refund; my case is the surge element only.

My own honest reading of F9 is that the notice states the 1.4× multiplier, a revised estimated fare of $29.75 and free cancellation, and that it was sent at 12:01:40 before the 12:02:00 trip start, so I do not contest D3; the remaining rider point is only that the stated estimate was higher than the sum finally charged, which SURGE-1 does not forbid.

Withdrawn as a supporting claim for any outcome: F14 (rider 746 d, 4.8, 0 disputes) and F15 (driver 2 upheld in 90 d) are profile facts and under TH-3/RD-6 they can never decide the case, so I drop them from my argument and rest my client's position on the fare records alone.

Both sides now read the notice as stating all three SURGE-1 items — the 1.4× multiplier, the revised estimated fare of $29.75 and free cancellation — in a log sent at 12:01:40, before the 12:02:00 trip start (F9); that reading, which the rider's own brief endorses, leaves no room for a refund under SURGE-2's 'rider not notified' row.

Profile facts cannot decide a finding (TH-3), and the rider's clean record (F14) does not outweigh the system log in F9; the driver's 2 upheld disputes in 90 days are neither route nor no-show matters (F15: route 0, no-show 0), so RD-6's precondition for a flag_account is absent.

The rider is right that the two chat messages are only pickup logistics (F10, F11, F12), but the notice duty in SURGE-1 is discharged through the in-app notice logged in F9, not through the chat thread, so the absence of fare talk in the chat proves nothing against the notice.

Conceded that the amount is under $10 and the records are complete and timestamped (F8, F9, F12), so the system may rule finally under TH-1/TH-2 — and on those complete records the notice requirement was met, which points to no_action rather than a refund.
